summary: Describes several problems found with the SIP non-INVITE transaction. It is an informational background document that sets out the issues which other work then addresses.

eli5.summary: A list of bugs found in how SIP handles certain requests. Fixes come in a separate memo.

questions: why sip non-invite transactions have issues
what are sip non-invite transaction problems
how does provisional response affect recovery
what is the non-invite race condition
subtitle: Six specific issues with non-INVITE transactions in SIP that cause timeouts and message loss.

tldr.problem: SIP non-INVITE transactions have a fixed, finite duration that creates race conditions, causing timing issues, message loss, and problems with failure detection.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies six specific problems: transactions must complete quickly or fail, provisional responses delay recovery, delayed responses cause temporary blacklisting, 408 responses arrive too late, timeouts doom forking proxies, and timer value mismatches worsen the issues.
tldr.outcome: This informational document identified the problems so that companion RFC 4320 could define solutions, such as prohibiting 408 responses to non-INVITE transactions and preventing proxies from forwarding late responses.

today: RFC 4321 is an Informational document that remains unchanged and has not been obsoleted. It continues to describe the core problems that companion RFC 4320 addresses with solutions.

sections.title: Introduction to the Problem
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) defines a non-INVITE transaction as a type of request that must complete within a fixed, finite time window (dependent on timer T1). This document describes six distinct problems created by this design.

Non-INVITE transactions include requests like OPTIONS, REGISTER, SUBSCRIBE and MESSAGE. The fixed-duration design was intended to prevent transactions from hanging indefinitely, but it creates edge cases where both the sender and receiver can end up with different views of whether the transaction succeeded.
sections.eli5: SIP has a timer that counts down for requests. If the answer doesn't come back in time, the sender thinks it failed. But sometimes the answer is just slow, not actually missing.

sections.title: The Core Race Condition
sections.content:
The fundamental problem: a User Agent Server (UAS) receiving a non-INVITE request has 64*T1 seconds to send a final response before the User Agent Client (UAC) times out and gives up. The problem is that the UAS cannot predict network propagation delays, so it cannot know how soon to send its response.

If the UAS waits too long, the UAC's 64*T1 timer fires, and the UAC abandons the transaction. When the UAS's response finally arrives, the UAC has no matching transaction to associate it with and discards it as spurious. The UAC and UAS disagree about whether the request succeeded.

To avoid losing this race, a UAS must send its final response as soon as possible, which constrains what kinds of processing it can perform during a non-INVITE transaction. Complex lookups or multi-step procedures are risky; the safest approach is to accept the request with 202 and send results in a separate request in the opposite direction.
sections.eli5: The sender gives the receiver 64 time units to answer. But the receiver doesn't know how fast the network is, so it can't tell if it's safe to do some work first. If it takes too long, the sender already left.

sections.title: Provisional Responses and Recovery Time
sections.content:
When a non-INVITE client transaction receives a provisional response (1xx), it moves from the Trying state to the Proceeding state. In Trying, the client retransmits every T1, doubling the interval each time. In Proceeding, it stops doubling and uses a fixed T2 interval instead.

If a provisional response arrives before Timer E has been doubled to T2 (which is T2/T1 = 8 times T1 by default), the transition to Proceeding cuts recovery time short. If the final response is lost and must be recovered through timeout and retransmission, the client now waits for Timer E to reach T2 instead of having already reached it. This can delay recovery from a lost final response by up to 3.5 seconds in deployed networks.
sections.eli5: When the receiver sends a 'I'm working on it' message back, the sender changes its resend timing. If this happens too early, it makes it take longer to notice if the final answer gets lost.

sections.title: Delayed Responses and Blacklisting
sections.content:
SIP elements use DNS Service Records (SRV) to discover and balance load across multiple servers. RFC 3263 specifies that when an element times out trying to reach a downstream element, it should try the next element from the SRV results and remember that the timed-out element failed temporarily.

Because non-INVITE transactions have a fixed duration, a proxy forwarding a non-INVITE request cannot retry it at a different downstream element within the same transaction. If the first element times out, the proxy's server transaction also times out before it can attempt a failover.

The combination creates a failure cascade: if an element fails to respond quickly enough, it gets temporarily blacklisted not just by its immediate peer, but by all upstream elements in the chain. Subsequent requests will avoid the failed element for a time, but the first request is still doomed.
sections.eli5: When a server doesn't answer in time, the system marks it as broken for a while. But because non-INVITE requests can't wait, the first request still fails even though future ones will avoid that server.

sections.title: Late 408 Responses and Forking Proxies
sections.content:
When a UAS times out waiting to send a final response before the UAC times out, it may send a 408 (Request Timeout) response. However, because the UAC has already abandoned the transaction, this 408 arrives at the next upstream element after that element's client transaction has also timed out. The upstream proxy must forward it statelessly, ensuring it arrives even later. In a chain of proxies, multiple 408s propagate back creating a response bombardment.

For forking proxies, the problem is different but equally severe: a single branch that sends a delayed or missing final response forces the proxy to wait for all branches to complete before selecting a 'best response'. This causes the proxy's server transaction to lose the race and timeout before it can forward any response back upstream.
sections.eli5: When a server takes too long to answer and sends a 'timeout' error, that error arrives so late that the sender already gave up. Multiple servers doing this create a flood of useless error messages.

sections.title: Timer Mismatches
sections.content:
The SIP specification defines default values for T1 (500 milliseconds) and T2 (4 seconds), but allows elements to configure different values. If two directly connected elements use different T1 or T2 values, the race condition in non-INVITE transactions becomes more likely to fail.

The specification provides no mechanism for elements to discover or negotiate each other's timer values. Deployers must carefully manage configurations to ensure that elements with non-default timer values never directly communicate with elements using default values.
sections.eli5: Different servers can have different timer settings. If they talk to each other and don't know each other's timers, the timing problems get worse.
